newsitem.title: USA: US senator circulates new flow control proposal.
newsitem.headline: US senator circulates new flow control proposal.

text.p: A key U.S. senator on Monday circulated a new flow control measure that generally would protect only those waste sites for which bonds were issued before the U.S. Supreme Court's landmark 1994 ruling on the issue, congressional aides said.

The draft bill prepared by Sen. John Chafee, R-R.I., chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, drew praise from municipal market representatives who see the measure as one of the last chances the market may have to protect billions of dollars of outstanding solid-waste facility debt nationwide.
"It's a very good sign," Micah Green, executive vice president of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association, said in a telephone interview.

"It's a limited bill. (But) all of us in the community need to realize that our only hope for relief from the Supreme Court decision is going to be narrow legislation such as the one proposed," Green added.

"We can work with this," Diane Shea, associate legislative director for environment for the National Association of Counties, told Reuters. "I'm feeling positive about it from a first glance. It protects bond issues in narrow categories."

The draft is almost identical to a narrow bill that House Commerce Committee Chairman Thomas Bliley, R-Va., crafted with input from major interest groups but that floundered during a House vote in January 1996.
It is far slimmer than a 1995 Senate version that fell under the weight of over 50 amendments tacked on to protect dozens of sites across the country for which bonds had not yet been issued.
A Chafee aide stressed that his boss' bill currently circulating on Capitol Hill is a "draft discussion document" and by no means a final proposal.
"This is not the final phase," the aide said. "It's the start of what we hope is going to be a short (period) of discussion prior to introduction."
The National Association of Counties' Shea expressed concern about one of the draft bill's provisions.
"The only kind of general obligation bond covered (by the bill) would be one where proceeds were used solely to finance one or more (flow control) facilities," Shea said.
That would exclude GO bonds issued for multiple purposes, Shea said.
